characters: Efua: a thirteen-year-old Ghanaian JHS student in a neat blue-and-white school uniform (or yellow apron when baking), practical, honest and determined.
Nana Ama: Efua’s wise grandmother in her sixties, wearing a warm patterned cloth and headwrap.
Auntie Dede: an experienced market trader who sells groundnuts and mentors Efua, wearing a vibrant green-and-gold dress.
Kwabena: Efua’s confident classmate in JHS uniform, quick to suggest risky shortcuts.

narrationPlan.voice: Mature, expressive Ghanaian English storyteller (`Kore`) for JHS 1–3.
notes: Fix any typo on page 3 before TTS generation and speak all cedi amounts clearly.

music: No background music by default for JHS text-first focus; optional soft piano toggle.
culturalNotes: Demonstrates sophisticated SME bookkeeping, working-capital management, and business ethics in a Ghanaian market and school-supply context.

pages.brief: Warm Ghanaian kitchen: Efua (13, yellow apron over blue-and-white dress) and Nana Ama (patterned cloth and headwrap) packing 100 neat wrapped portions of golden groundnut cakes into trays.
pages.narration: Warm, upbeat continuation of Efua’s journey. Clear pronunciation of "Efua", "Nana Ama", and "nkate".

pages.brief: Veranda scene: Efua holding up her notebook with a huge celebratory smile while Nana Ama sits on a stool watching her with a calm, thoughtful expression.
Close medium shot of Efua looking worriedly into a small open metal cash tin on the wooden table containing only a few cedi notes, while Nana Ama walks over.
pages.narration: Sudden drop from excitement to shock and confusion.

pages.brief: Nana Ama sitting calmly with Efua at the table, opening a large ruled accounting ledger beside small paper receipts and a calculator.
pages.narration: Calm, reassuring authority from Nana Ama.

pages.brief: Close view of Efua writing neatly in her ledger book with a ruler and pen (no readable text on the image) as Nana Ama points to the top line.
pages.narration: Clear distinction between "revenue", "variable costs", and "fixed costs".

pages.brief: Efua pressing buttons on a desktop calculator beside sacks of groundnuts and small paper receipts while Nana Ama checks the figures.
pages.narration: Read the numbers clearly: "one hundred and ten plus thirty equals one hundred and forty cedis".

pages.brief: Nana Ama pointing to two neat columns in the open ledger while Efua writes the total with an expression of sudden understanding.
pages.narration: Clear step-by-step arithmetic: "one hundred and forty plus twenty-five gives one hundred and sixty-five cedis".

pages.brief: Efua holding her ledger in one hand and looking into the cash tin with the other, asking Nana Ama a thoughtful question.
pages.narration: Crucial pivot from accounting profit to cash flow!

pages.brief: Busy Ghanaian market stall with sacks of groundnuts: Auntie Dede (vibrant green-and-gold dress) speaking warmly to Efua, who claps a hand to her forehead in sudden realization.
pages.narration: Aha-moment energy on "difference between accounting profit and cash flow".

pages.brief: Auntie Dede arranging three small wooden bowls on her market counter to illustrate Cash In, Cash Out, and Credit Owed for Efua.
pages.narration: Clear, practical breakdown of the cash-flow crunch (`200 − 60 = 140` cash in vs `165` cash out).

pages.brief: Sunny town street: Kwabena leaning on his bicycle talking to Efua, who stands tall holding her ledger and shakes her head firmly with integrity.
pages.narration: Sly, casual tone for Kwabena; firm, principled refusal from Efua.

pages.brief: Sunny veranda: Efua, Nana Ama and Auntie Dede smiling proudly around the table with a neat balanced ledger, trays of groundnut cakes, and a separate savings jar for emergencies (no text on image).
pages.narration: Confident, satisfying conclusion. Gentle pause before "The end".

teacherGuide.overview: Serving as both a standalone JHS entrepreneurship story and a direct sequel to Efua’s Honest Business, this 12-page story teaches essential real-world financial management: why sales growth can trigger a cash-flow crisis, how to separate revenue from variable and fixed costs, how credit sales affect cash flow versus accounting profit, why emergency reserves matter for external shocks (like rainstorms or price rises), and why ethical marketing outperforms deception.
learningGoals: Distinguish clearly between revenue (total sales), expenses (variable + fixed costs), and net profit.
Explain the difference between accounting profit and cash flow, showing how unpaid credit sales can starve a profitable business of working capital.
Calculate unit variable costs, total costs, net profit, and net cash flow from a realistic Ghana cedi scenario.
Evaluate ethical versus deceptive responses to rising business costs.

beforeReading: Ask learners: "If a shopkeeper sells 200 cedis worth of goods in a week, did the shopkeeper make 200 cedis of profit? Why or why not?"
whileReading: Pause after page 8 to write Efua’s Income Statement on the board: Revenue (200) − Variable Costs (140) − Fixed Costs (25) = Profit (35).
Pause after page 10 to write Efua’s Cash Flow Statement alongside it: Cash In (200 − 60 credit = 140) − Cash Out (165 expenses + 10 snacks = 175) = −35 cash change!
afterReading: Have learners work in pairs to calculate Efua’s new weekly profit after she lowers her ingredient cost from 1.10 cedis to 0.90 cedis per pack (see Maths Extension).
discussion: Why do many promising small businesses get into trouble right when their orders suddenly grow larger?
How did Wednesday’s rainstorm (requiring a 30-cedi taxi) show that financial difficulties can come from unexpected external events rather than laziness?
Why was requiring a 50% cash deposit on bulk canteen orders fair to both Efua and the school canteen?
reflection: How can separating "money coming in", "expenses to pay", and "emergency savings" help a family or student club manage money wisely?

mathsExtension.task: In the following week, Efua sells 100 packs at 2 cedis each (200 cedis revenue). Her wholesale ingredient cost is now 0.90 cedis per pack (90 cedis), there is no taxi emergency (0 cedis), and fixed costs are 25 cedis. What are her new total expenses and new weekly profit?
mathsExtension.answer: Total expenses = 90 + 25 = 115 cedis; New profit = 200 − 115 = 85 cedis.

mathsExtension.task: Under her new rule, the school canteen orders 30 packs (60 cedis total) and pays a 50% deposit upfront. How much cash does Efua receive immediately when the order is placed?

support: Use play cedi notes and three labelled envelopes ("Ingredients & Rent", "Unpaid IOU Note", "My Profit") to act out pages 6–10.
stretch: Prepare a two-column comparison table explaining 4 differences between an Income Statement (Revenue & Profit) and a Cash Flow Statement (Cash In & Cash Out).

culturalNotes: Builds directly on the characters of Efua, Nana Ama, Kwabena, and Auntie Dede from Efua’s Honest Business while remaining completely understandable on its own.
localiseThis: Invite learners to identify fixed costs and variable costs for a familiar local enterprise (such as a seamstress shop, barbering salon, kenkey kitchen, or provision store).

pronunciation.guidance: three soft syllables, "eh-FOO-ah". A two-syllable "EH-fwah" is also heard in English speech.
reviewerNotes: Choose between "eh-FOO-ah" (3 syllables) and "EH-fwah" (2) for the narrator voice.
Supply IPA and mark tone if wanted.
Confirm spelling (nkate / nkatie) and pronunciation before this term is used in a published story.
Confirm vowel quality and whether the final syllable is stressed.
Confirm language of origin and meaning before it appears in teacher notes.
